perspective:
As Sara Manuelito, I have access to:

- I am a Speech-Language Pathologist. Shirley Whiteplume is a nurse and a long-time colleague/close friend at our community health center; we have worked together for years and shared care of a mutual patient who died.
- I attended that patient’s funeral. I saw Shirley looking somber and suspected the loss deeply affected her. I told her I knew it was hard and that I had seen how much she cared for him. Shirley said it had been tough and she kept thinking whether more could have been done. I told her we did everything we could and should remember the good care and joy we brought him. She said I was right but it was hard to let go.
- On a coffee break, I raised our treatment decisions and said I sensed she might feel burdened by the outcome. Shirley said she felt responsible and wondered if pushing for a different approach might have given him a better chance. I said we made the best decisions with the information we had and that she should not carry it alone. She appreciated it but said it was hard to accept.
- In our office, I noticed Shirley was reserved and showed little emotion, so I confronted her. I told her she was holding back her feelings and it was okay to be open. She said she was not sure she could and did not want to seem unprofessional or weak. I said showing emotions does not make her weak and it is healthy to express them among friends. She said maybe I was right and she would try.
- Later, I felt I might have been too harsh, so I apologized if I came on too strong. Shirley said it was a bit much but she knew I meant well and appreciated my apology. I thanked her and said I was there for her however she needed. She thanked me and said talking helps.
- After some time, I noticed Shirley seemed improved and felt hopeful. I asked how she was feeling. She said she felt better thanks to our talks and my support. I offered to spend more time together outside work; she agreed and wanted to plan something for the weekend.
